meta.ogDescription: Napoleon's documented line was "impossible n'est pas français" (1813). The "dictionary of fools" version is a later embellishment nobody can source.

answer.label: Not Napoleon’s words — a later paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French & military commander
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment is authentically Napoleon’s: in a letter of 9 July 1813 to General Le Marois, defending Magdeburg, he wrote — in the standard telling — “Ce n’est pas possible, m’écrivez-vous : cela n’est pas français” (“It is not possible, you write to me: that is not French”), later compressed to “impossible n’est pas français.” But this ornate English sentence about a “dictionary of fools” matches none of his documented statements and traces to no primary source — it is a much later paraphrase.

source.excerpt: Ce n’est pas possible, m’écrivez-vous : cela n’est pas français.
trail: The saying Napoleon is actually documented using is “impossible n’est pas français”, traced to a July 1813 letter to General Le Marois and popularized by Balzac in 1838, per French Wikipedia.

A survey of the origins notes two competing accounts (Somosierra 1808 and the 1813 Le Marois letter) and stresses “there are no confirmed sources” — and none mention a “dictionary of fools”, per The Connexion.
The embellished “dictionnaire des imbéciles / dictionary of fools” form circulates widely as a Napoleon quote on aggregators such as citation-celebre.com, but with no documented source attached.
source.excerptNote: The line as traditionally reported from Napoleon’s 1813 letter to General Le Marois — “It is not possible, you write to me: that is not French.” Note that it names no “dictionary” and no “fools.”

source.rightsNote: Napoleon’s documented French line (“impossible n’est pas français,” from an 1813 letter) is long in the public domain. But the specific English wording — “a word to be found only in the dictionary of fools” — cannot be tied to any identifiable first publication or translator, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it.

author.heading: About Napoleon Bonaparte
author.metaLine: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French & military commander
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from Corsican artillery officer to Emperor of the French, reshaping Europe through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars before his defeat at Waterloo in 1815 and exile to Saint Helena. His terse, combative maxims — often recorded second-hand by aides and memoirists — made him one of history’s most quoted figures, and one of the most freely misquoted.

misattribution.heading: How the wording drifted
misattribution.intro: This is a case where the thought is real but the sentence is invented. Napoleon did dismiss the word “impossible” — but not in these words.

items.why: No letter, memoir, or speech records Napoleon saying “a word to be found only in the dictionary of fools.” Origin surveys list only the “impossible n’est pas français” accounts and note there are “no confirmed sources,” per The Connexion.
Napoleon really did reject “impossible”: in an 1813 letter to General Le Marois he wrote that the word “n’est pas français,” a line Balzac later popularized in 1838, per French Wikipedia.

misattribution.truthLine: Napoleon’s real, documented line was “impossible n’est pas français” — “impossible is not French” — from his 1813 letter to General Le Marois; the “dictionary of fools” sentence is a later English embellishment with no source, as the origin record shows.

context.heading: Why the line stuck to Napoleon
lead: Napoleon is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for tidy, motivational one-liners: a decisive conqueror is the perfect mouthpiece for “nothing is impossible.” His genuine remark — a sharp play on the word français in a wartime dispatch — is punchier in French than in English, so translators and anthologists reshaped it. Over time the untranslatable pun (“not French”) was swapped for a portable moral (“the dictionary of fools”).
The result reads like Napoleon and flatters the same defiant spirit, which is exactly why it spread — and why it is worth flagging that the words themselves are not his.
context.pull: The idea is Napoleon’s. The sentence is someone else’s.
